blocks.title: Client vs Proxy Routing
items: Client-side hashing: fastest, no extra hop.
Proxy (Envoy, twemproxy, mcrouter): central routing + failover.
Proxy costs a hop, buys one place to fix things.
One hot key expires; N concurrent requests all miss.
All N hit the DB for the same value at the same instant.
Spike scales with concurrency, not with traffic growth.
Also called thundering herd or dogpile.
Go's singleflight and Caffeine's LoadingCache do this per key.
Lock TTL must exceed the load, or the herd returns.
XFetch: refresh early with probability rising near the TTL.
One request refreshes before the cliff, not all of them.
No locks, no coordination, no wait.
Keep logical expiry inside the value; the key has no TTL.
Always serve the value, even when logically stale.
Trigger an async refresh when it goes logically stale.
Requests for IDs that do not exist in the DB either.
Scrapers and enumeration attacks always miss, always reach DB.
Fix 1: negative cache the not-found with a short TTL.
Fix 2: Bloom filter of existing IDs rejects unknowns in O(1).

blocks.title: Bloom Errs the Right Way
blocks.text: No false negatives, tunable false positives. A false positive costs one wasted DB lookup — the acceptable direction to be wrong.

Fixes: TTL jitter, staged warmup, rate limit at the origin.
Circuit breakers so the DB sheds load instead of dying.

blocks.title: Plan for h = 0
blocks.text: Cold start after failover is avalanche with a different trigger. A cache the system cannot survive without is not a cache — it is an undeclared dependency.

blocks.title: Two More Landmines
items: Multi-MB blobs block the Redis event loop on write.
Split, compress, or offload to object storage + CDN.
Key omitting tenant/user leaks data across users.
Put the full authorization context in the key. Always.

blocks.title: The Whole Handbook, One Line
blocks.text: A cache is a bounded, expiring, evictable copy. TTL bounds how wrong it can be, eviction bounds how big it can get, invalidation bounds how long it stays wrong — and every pattern choice is just where you put the write.

caption.text: Part 2 of CACHING IN SYSTEM DESIGN. Most "add a cache" answers stop at Redis — but the interview (and the incident) is decided by what happens when the key expires. 10 pages of handwritten notes: the read/write patterns, TTL mechanics and jitter, how LRU/LFU/W-TinyLFU actually evict, invalidation that survives races, and the failure modes — stampede, penetration, avalanche — with the fix for each. Save it before your next system design round.
